Towards a Characterization of Matrix Monotonicity via Radial Convexity

Abstract.

The theory of matrix monotone functions of finite degree depends subtly on the matrix size. Motivated by this phenomenon, we introduce radial convexity of metrics with respect to matrix orders on the cone of positive definite matrices. We establish radial convexity of several natural metrics with respect to the Loewner order and then focus on the Frobenius norm. Using the Daleckii-Krein formula, we relate radial convexity to the positivity of the Hadamard square of the corresponding Loewner matrix. This leads us to conjecture that radial convexity of order nn is equivalent to matrix monotonicity of degree nn, and we prove this equivalence in degree 22. We further provide evidence in higher dimensions, obtain a characterization in degree 33, and discuss extensions of our results to arbitrary unitarily invariant norms.

Key words and phrases:
Radially Convex, Matrix Monotone, Loewner Matrix, Hadamard Product
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary: 47A64; Secondary: 15B33, 15B48.

1. Introduction

In matrix analysis and operator theory there are two hallmark concepts that undergird the study of several interesting objects. These two concepts are the idea of operator or matrix monotonicity and the study of the geometry of the cone of positive operators or positive definite matrices via different metrics. It should not be surprising that these two concepts have been intertwined in the study of matrix analysis.

The study of means of positive definite matrices is closely connected with monotonicity. A consequence of the operator monotonicity of the associated function to a Kubo-Ando mean is the natural order-theoretic in-betweenness property

A≤A​σ​B≤B.{\rm A}\leq{\rm A}\sigma{\rm B}\leq{\rm B}\,.

This property plays an important role in the theory of Kubo-Ando means and provides a direct matrix analogue of scalar betweenness.

The geometry connection comes with the geometric in-betweenness proposed by Audenaert in the study of matrix means that do not necessarily satisfy the axioms of Kubo-Ando theory [1]. In this approach, the order relation is replaced by a metric condition, requiring the mean to lie metrically between its arguments. Given a metric d{\rm d} on the cone ℙn\mathbb{P}_{n} of positive definite n×nn\times n matrices,, geometric in-betweenness is expressed by the conditions

d⁡(A,A​σ​B)≤d⁡(A,B) and d⁡(B,A​σ​B)≤d⁡(A,B).{\rm d}({\rm A},{\rm A}\sigma{\rm B})\leq{\rm d}({\rm A},{\rm B})\qquad\text{ and }\qquad{\rm d}({\rm B},{\rm A}\sigma{\rm B})\leq{\rm d}({\rm A},{\rm B})\,.

At first sight, one might expect order-theoretic in-betweenness to imply geometric in-betweenness. This is indeed the case for several familiar geometries on ℙn\mathbb{P}_{n}. Consider the case of an ff-metric induced by a matrix monotone function ff of degree nn as follows,

d∥⋅∥,f(A,B):=‖f(A)−f(B)‖{\rm d}_{\|\cdot\|,f}({\rm A},{\rm B}):=\left\|f({\rm A})-f({\rm B})\right\|

for a unitarily invariant norm ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\|. Then

A≤C≤B⟹f⁡(A)≤f⁡(C)≤f⁡(B)orf⁡(A)≥f⁡(C)≥f⁡(B),{\rm A}\leq{\rm C}\leq{\rm B}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad f({\rm A})\leq f({\rm C})\leq f({\rm B})\,\quad\text{or}\quad f({\rm A})\geq f({\rm C})\geq f({\rm B}),

which implies that

d‖⋅‖,f​(A,C)≤d‖⋅‖,f​(A,B)andd‖⋅‖,f​(B,C)≤d‖⋅‖,f​(A,B).{\rm d}_{\left\|\cdot\right\|,f}({\rm A},{\rm C})\leq{\rm d}_{\left\|\cdot\right\|,f}({\rm A},{\rm B})\,\quad\text{and}\quad{\rm d}_{\left\|\cdot\right\|,f}({\rm B},{\rm C})\leq{\rm d}_{\left\|\cdot\right\|,f}({\rm A},{\rm B}).

See Proposition 3.9 for more details. This class includes many familiar metrics from matrix analysis, such as those induced by unitarily invariant norms, the Hellinger metric, and the chaotic Thompson metric.

However, the example f⁡(x)=x2f(x)=x^{2} shows that an ff-metric need not be compatible with the Loewner order: even if

A≤C≤B,{\rm A}\leq{\rm C}\leq{\rm B}\,,

it may happen that

d⁡(A,C)>d⁡(A,B).{\rm d}({\rm A},{\rm C})>{\rm d}({\rm A},{\rm B})\,.

Thus, geometric in-betweenness does not follow from the order relation alone, but depends on the compatibility between the metric d{\rm d} and the order structure of ℙn\mathbb{P}_{n}. This leads naturally to the question when does the order relation imply the geometric relation.

This question has been studied in the setting of partially ordered metric spaces, where such spaces are said to be radially convex (see [10] and the references therein). In view of the broader types of spaces that arise in matrix analysis and operator theory, we adopt the following more general definition.

Definition 1.1 (Radial Convexity).

Let 𝒳\mathcal{X} be a set equipped with a binary relation ⪯\preceq, and let

d:𝒳×𝒳⟶[0,∞){\rm d}:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}\longrightarrow[0,\infty)

be a nonnegative function. We say that d{\rm d} is radially convex with respect to ⪯\preceq if

A⪯C⪯B{\rm A}\preceq{\rm C}\preceq{\rm B}

implies

d⁡(A,C)≤d⁡(A,B) and d⁡(C,B)≤d⁡(A,B).{\rm d}({\rm A},{\rm C})\leq{\rm d}({\rm A},{\rm B})\qquad\text{ and }\qquad{\rm d}({\rm C},{\rm B})\leq{\rm d}({\rm A},{\rm B})\,.
Remark 1.2.

In the above definition, ⪯\preceq is not required to be a partial order and d{\rm d} is not required to be a metric. This additional generality is useful in matrix analysis, where several natural relations are order-like without being partial orders, and where nonnegative divergences frequently arise in place of metrics.

Moreover, if D=d2{\rm D}={\rm d}^{2}, then radial convexity with respect to d{\rm d} is equivalent to radial convexity with respect to D{\rm D}, since the function t↦t2t\mapsto t^{2} is increasing on [0,∞)\left[0,\infty\right). This observation will allow us to work interchangeably with a metric and its square when convenient.

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 contains the necessary preliminaries on the Loewner order, matrix monotone functions, and Loewner matrices. In Section 3, we establish radial convexity for several natural metrics on ℙn\mathbb{P}_{n}. We then show that matrix monotonicity provides a general mechanism for radial convexity. More precisely, if ff is matrix monotone of degree nn and ‖⋅‖\left\|\cdot\right\| is a unitarily invariant norm, then the metric

d‖⋅‖,f​(A,B)=‖f⁡(A)−f⁡(B)‖d_{\left\|\cdot\right\|,f}({\rm A},{\rm B})=\left\|f({\rm A})-f({\rm B})\right\|

is radially convex with respect to the Loewner order on ℙn\mathbb{P}_{n}.

This provides a large family of metrics for which order-theoretic in-betweenness implies metric in-betweenness, and includes several classical geometries on the cone of positive definite matrices.

In Section 4, we investigate the converse implication, concentrating on the metric induced by the Frobenius norm. In this case, the Hilbert space structure of the Frobenius norm allows us to obtain a characterization of radial convexity. From this point on, since the Frobenius norm is fixed, we simply say that ff is radially convex of order nn if the metric induced by ff is radially convex with respect to the Loewner order on ℙn\mathbb{P}_{n}. More precisely, radial convexity implies that

Re​⟨D​f​(A)​(X),D​f​(A)​(Y)⟩F≥0{\rm Re}\left\langle{\rm D}f({\rm A})({\rm X}),{\rm D}f({\rm A})({\rm Y})\right\rangle_{{\rm F}}\geq 0

for every A∈ℙn{\rm A}\in\mathbb{P}_{n} and every X,Y≥0{\rm X},{\rm Y}\geq 0. Using the Daleckii-Krein formula

D​f​(A)​(H)=Lf​(A)∘H,{\rm D}f({\rm A})({\rm H})={\rm L}_{f}({\rm A})\circ{\rm H}\,,

we translate this differential condition into a condition on the Loewner matrix Lf​(A){\rm L}_{f}({\rm A}) (see Definition 2.9). In particular, radial convexity implies

Lf​(A)∘Lf​(A)≥0{\rm L}_{f}({\rm A})\circ{\rm L}_{f}({\rm A})\geq 0

for every A∈ℙn{\rm A}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}, where ∘\circ denotes the Hadamard product. Thus, the converse problem is closely related to the question of when positivity of the Hadamard square of a Loewner matrix forces positivity of the Loewner matrix itself.

The results obtained in this paper for the Frobenius norm are summarized in the following diagram.

These results lead us to the following conjecture.

Conjecture.

Let f:(0,∞)→ℝf:\left(0,\infty\right)\to\mathbb{R}. Then ff is radially convex of order nn (with respect to the Frobenius norm) if and only if ff is matrix monotone of degree nn .

We prove this in degree 22. Indeed, in this case positivity of Lf​(A)∘Lf​(A){\rm L}_{f}({\rm A})\circ{\rm L}_{f}({\rm A}) forces positivity of Lf​(A){\rm L}_{f}({\rm A}), and hence radial convexity of order 22 is equivalent to matrix monotonicity of degree 22. In degree 33, we show that radial convexity already provides the principal minor conditions required for matrix monotonicity, leaving the sign of the determinant of the Loewner matrix as the remaining obstruction. We also give explicit higher-dimensional examples supporting the conjecture. Finally, Section 5 contains concluding remarks and investigates to what extent the degree 22 result persists for arbitrary unitarily invariant norms.

2. Preliminaries

In this section, we recall some basic facts concerning Hermitian matrices, the Loewner order, and operator/matrix monotone functions. Throughout this paper, we denote by Mat⁡(n):=Mat⁡(n,ℂ){\rm Mat}(n):={\rm Mat}(n,\mathbb{C}) the algebra of n×nn\times n matrices with complex entries.

We denote by Un{\rm U}_{n} the unitary group

Un:={g∈Mat⁡(n),g​g∗=Idn},{\rm U}_{n}:=\left\{g\in{\rm Mat}(n)\,,gg^{*}={\rm Id}_{n}\right\},

and by ℍn\mathbb{H}_{n} the real vector space of Hermitian matrices of size nn,

ℍn:={X∈Mat⁡(n),X∗=X}.\mathbb{H}_{n}:=\left\{{\rm X}\in{\rm Mat}(n)\,,{\rm X}^{*}={\rm X}\right\}.

Recall that for every A∈ℍn{\rm A}\in\mathbb{H}_{n}, there exists a unitary matrix U∈Un{\rm U}\in{\rm U}_{n} and real numbers λ1,…,λn\lambda_{1}\,,\ldots\,,\lambda_{n} such that

A=Udiag⁡(λ1,…,λn)​U∗,{\rm A}={\rm U}{\rm diag}(\lambda_{1}\,,\ldots\,,\lambda_{n}){\rm U}^{*},

so that the spectrum of a Hermitian matrix is contained in ℝ\mathbb{R}. Similarly, we denote by ℍn+\mathbb{H}^{+}_{n} and ℙn\mathbb{P}_{n} the subsets of ℍn\mathbb{H}_{n} given by

ℍn+:={X∈ℍn,X≥0},ℙn:={X∈ℍn,X>0}.\mathbb{H}^{+}_{n}:=\left\{{\rm X}\in\mathbb{H}_{n}\,,{\rm X}\geq 0\right\}\,,\qquad\mathbb{P}_{n}:=\left\{{\rm X}\in\mathbb{H}_{n}\,,{\rm X}>0\right\}\,.
Definition 2.1.

Let A,B∈ℙn{\rm A}\,,{\rm B}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}. We say that A{\rm A} is smaller than or equal to B{\rm B} with respect to the Loewner order, and write A≤B{\rm A}\leq{\rm B}, if B−A∈ℍn+{\rm B}-{\rm A}\in\mathbb{H}^{+}_{n} .

Remark 2.2.

Similarly, we write A<B{\rm A}<{\rm B} whenever B−A∈ℙn{\rm B}-{\rm A}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}. Notice that the Loewner order ≤\leq is defined on the entire space ℍn\mathbb{H}_{n}, although in this paper we will be primarily interested in its restriction to the positive definite cone ℙn\mathbb{P}_{n} .

Let f:I→ℝf:{\rm I}\to\mathbb{R} be a continuous function, where I{\rm I} is a subinterval of (0,∞)(0,\infty). If A∈ℍn{\rm A}\in\mathbb{H}_{n} satisfies Spec⁡(A)⊆I{\rm Spec}({\rm A})\subseteq{\rm I}, the functional calculus allows us to define f⁡(A)f({\rm A}). Indeed, if

A=Udiag⁡(λ1,…,λn)​U∗,{\rm A}={\rm U}{\rm diag}(\lambda_{1}\,,\ldots\,,\lambda_{n}){\rm U}^{*}\,,

then

f⁡(A):=Udiag⁡(f⁡(λ1),…,f⁡(λn))​U∗.f({\rm A}):={\rm U}{\rm diag}\left(f(\lambda_{1})\,,\ldots\,,f(\lambda_{n})\right){\rm U}^{*}\,.

This definition does not depend on the choice of the unitary diagonalization of A{\rm A}. We now recall the notion of an operator monotone function .

Definition 2.3.

Let I⊆ℝ{\rm I}\subseteq\mathbb{R} be an interval. A function f:I⟶ℝf:{\rm I}\longrightarrow\mathbb{R} is said to be operator monotone increasing if, for every n≥1n\geq 1 and every A,B∈ℍn{\rm A}\,,{\rm B}\in\mathbb{H}_{n} such that Spec⁡(A),Spec⁡(B)⊆I{\rm Spec}({\rm A})\,,{\rm Spec}({\rm B})\subseteq{\rm I} and A≤B{\rm A}\leq{\rm B}, we have

f⁡(A)≤f⁡(B).f({\rm A})\leq f({\rm B})\,.

Similarly, ff is said to be operator monotone decreasing if

A≤B⟹f⁡(A)≥f⁡(B){\rm A}\leq{\rm B}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad f({\rm A})\geq f({\rm B})

for every n≥1n\geq 1 and every A,B∈ℍn{\rm A}\,,{\rm B}\in\mathbb{H}_{n} with spectra contained in I{\rm I} .

Remark 2.4.

Clearly, ff is operator monotone decreasing if and only if −f-f is operator monotone increasing. When no confusion can arise, we will simply say that ff is operator monotone if it is operator monotone in one of these two directions .

In this paper, we will mainly consider functions defined on the positive half-line

f:(0,∞)⟶ℝ,f:\left(0,\infty\right)\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}\,,

and hence the functional calculus will be applied to matrices in ℙn\mathbb{P}_{n} for all nn .

Notation 2.5.

For a continuously differentiable function f:I⟶ℝf:{\rm I}\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}, and A∈ℙn{\rm A}\in\mathbb{P}_{n} such that Spec⁡(A)⊆I{\rm Spec}({\rm A})\subseteq{\rm I}, we denote by

D​f​(A):ℍn⟶ℍn{\rm D}f({\rm A}):\mathbb{H}_{n}\longrightarrow\mathbb{H}_{n}

the Fréchet derivative of the matrix function induced by ff at A{\rm A}, i.e.

D​f​(A)​(H)=limt→0f⁡(A+t​H)−f⁡(A)t,(H∈ℍn).{\rm D}f({\rm A})({\rm H})=\lim\limits_{t\to 0}\frac{f({\rm A}+t{\rm H})-f({\rm A})}{t}\,,\qquad\left({\rm H}\in\mathbb{H}_{n}\right)\,.

We recall a differential characterization of operator monotone functions (see [3]) .

Proposition 2.6.

Let f:I→ℝf:{\rm I}\to\mathbb{R} be continuously differentiable. Then ff is operator monotone increasing if and only if, for every n≥1n\geq 1, every A∈ℙn{\rm A}\in\mathbb{P}_{n} with Spec⁡(A)⊆I{\rm Spec}({\rm A})\subseteq{\rm I}, and every H∈ℍn+{\rm H}\in\mathbb{H}^{+}_{n},

D​f​(A)​(H)≥0.{\rm D}f({\rm A})({\rm H})\geq 0\,.

Similarly, ff is operator monotone decreasing if and only if

D​f​(A)​(H)≤0{\rm D}f({\rm A})({\rm H})\leq 0

for every n≥1n\geq 1, every A∈ℙn{\rm A}\in\mathbb{P}_{n} with Spec⁡(A)⊆I{\rm Spec}({\rm A})\subseteq{\rm I}, and every H∈ℍn+{\rm H}\in\mathbb{H}^{+}_{n} .

Proof.

See [3] (see also [5]) .

∎

Lemma 2.7.

Let A∈ℙn{\rm A}\in\mathbb{P}_{n} and suppose that A=P​Δ​P∗{\rm A}={\rm P}\Delta{\rm P}^{*}, where Δ\Delta is diagonal and P∈Un{\rm P}\in{\rm U}_{n}. Then

D​f​(A)​(H)=PD​f​(Δ)​(P∗​HP)​P∗,(H∈ℍn+).{\rm D}f({\rm A})({\rm H})={\rm P}{\rm D}f(\Delta)({\rm P}^{*}{\rm H}{\rm P}){\rm P}^{*}\,,\qquad\left({\rm H}\in\mathbb{H}^{+}_{n}\right).

In particular, D​f​(A)​(H)≥0{\rm D}f({\rm A})({\rm H})\geq 0 for all H∈ℍn+{\rm H}\in\mathbb{H}^{+}_{n} if and only if D​f​(Δ)​(X)≥0{\rm D}f(\Delta)({\rm X})\geq 0 for all X∈ℍn+{\rm X}\in\mathbb{H}^{+}_{n} .

Proof.

We have

D​f​(A)​(H)\displaystyle{\rm D}f({\rm A})({\rm H}) =\displaystyle= limt→0f⁡(A+t​H)−f⁡(A)t=limt→0f⁡(A+t​H)−f⁡(A)t\displaystyle\lim\limits_{t\to 0}\frac{f({\rm A}+t{\rm H})-f({\rm A})}{t}=\lim\limits_{t\to 0}\frac{f({\rm A}+t{\rm H})-f({\rm A})}{t}
=\displaystyle= limt→0f⁡(P​Δ​P∗+t​H)−f⁡(P​Δ​P∗)t\displaystyle\lim\limits_{t\to 0}\frac{f({\rm P}\Delta{\rm P}^{*}+t{\rm H})-f({\rm P}\Delta{\rm P}^{*})}{t}
=\displaystyle= limt→0f⁡(P​Δ​P∗+t​PP∗​HPP∗)−f⁡(P​Δ​P∗)t\displaystyle\lim\limits_{t\to 0}\frac{f({\rm P}\Delta{\rm P}^{*}+t{\rm P}{\rm P}^{*}{\rm H}{\rm P}{\rm P}^{*})-f({\rm P}\Delta{\rm P}^{*})}{t}
=\displaystyle= P⁡(limt→0f⁡(Δ+t​P∗​HP)−f⁡(Δ)t)​P∗\displaystyle{\rm P}\left(\lim\limits_{t\to 0}\frac{f(\Delta+t{\rm P}^{*}{\rm H}{\rm P})-f(\Delta)}{t}\right){\rm P}^{*}
=\displaystyle= PD​f​(Δ)​(P∗​HP)​P∗.\displaystyle{\rm P}{\rm D}f(\Delta)({\rm P}^{*}{\rm H}{\rm P}){\rm P}^{*}\,.

∎

Corollary 2.8.

The function ff is operator monotone increasing if and only if, for every n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, every diagonal matrix Δ∈ℙn\Delta\in\mathbb{P}_{n}, and every H∈ℍn+{\rm H}\in\mathbb{H}^{+}_{n}, we have

D​f​(Δ)​(H)≥0.{\rm D}f(\Delta)({\rm H})\geq 0\,.

We now recall the definition of the Loewner matrix associated with a differentiable function f:(0,∞)→ℝf:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R} and a diagonal matrix D=diag⁡(λi)∈ℙn{\rm D}={\rm diag}(\lambda_{i})\in\mathbb{P}_{n} (see [3]). For all x,y∈(0,∞)x,y\in\left(0\,,\infty\right), we define the first divided difference of ff by

f[1]​(x,y)={f⁡(x)−f⁡(y)x−y if ​x≠yf′​(x) if ​x=yf^{[1]}(x,y)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{f(x)-f(y)}{x-y}&\text{ if }x\neq y\\ f^{\prime}(x)&\text{ if }x=y\end{cases}
Definition 2.9.

For ff as above and D=diag⁡(λ1,…,λn)∈ℙn{\rm D}={\rm diag}(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{n})\in\mathbb{P}_{n}, the Loewner matrix associated with ff and D{\rm D} is defined by

Lf​(D)=(f[1]​(λi,λj))1≤i,j≤n.{\rm L}_{f}({\rm D})=\left(f^{[1]}(\lambda_{i},\lambda_{j})\right)_{1\leq i,j\leq n}.

If the eigenvalues λ1,…,λn\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{n} are pairwise distinct, then

Lf​(D)=(f′​(λ1)f⁡(λ1)−f⁡(λ2)λ1−λ2⋯f⁡(λ1)−f⁡(λn)λ1−λnf⁡(λ2)−f⁡(λ1)λ2−λ1f′​(λ2)⋯f⁡(λ2)−f⁡(λn)λ2−λn⋱f⁡(λn)−f⁡(λ1)λn−λ1f⁡(λn)−f⁡(λ2)λn−λ2⋯f′​(λn)).{\rm L}_{f}({\rm D})=\begin{pmatrix}f^{\prime}(\lambda_{1})&\displaystyle\frac{f(\lambda_{1})-f(\lambda_{2})}{\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{2}}&\cdots&\displaystyle\frac{f(\lambda_{1})-f(\lambda_{n})}{\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{n}}\\ \displaystyle\frac{f(\lambda_{2})-f(\lambda_{1})}{\lambda_{2}-\lambda_{1}}&f^{\prime}(\lambda_{2})&\cdots&\displaystyle\frac{f(\lambda_{2})-f(\lambda_{n})}{\lambda_{2}-\lambda_{n}}\\ \vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\ \displaystyle\frac{f(\lambda_{n})-f(\lambda_{1})}{\lambda_{n}-\lambda_{1}}&\displaystyle\frac{f(\lambda_{n})-f(\lambda_{2})}{\lambda_{n}-\lambda_{2}}&\cdots&f^{\prime}(\lambda_{n})\end{pmatrix}\,.
Remark 2.10.

Let A∈ℙn{\rm A}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}. By the spectral theorem, there exist U∈Un{\rm U}\in{\rm U}_{n} and a diagonal matrix D=diag⁡(λi){\rm D}={\rm diag}\left(\lambda_{i}\right), with λi>0\lambda_{i}>0, such that A=UDU∗{\rm A}={\rm U}{\rm D}{\rm U}^{*}. We will write

Lf​(A):=Lf​(D).{\rm L}_{f}({\rm A}):={\rm L}_{f}({\rm D})\,.

This notation depends on the ordering of the eigenvalues of A{\rm A}. However, a different ordering only produces a simultaneous permutation of the rows and columns of Lf​(A){\rm L}_{f}({\rm A}). In particular, properties such as

Lf​(A)≥0 or Lf​(A)∘Lf​(A)≥0{\rm L}_{f}({\rm A})\geq 0\qquad\text{ or }\qquad{\rm L}_{f}({\rm A})\circ{\rm L}_{f}({\rm A})\geq 0

are independent of the ordering of the eigenvalues .

Remark 2.11.

Let A=(ai,j){\rm A}=\left(a_{i,j}\right) and B=(bi,j){\rm B}=\left(b_{i,j}\right) be two matrices in Mat⁡(n){\rm Mat}(n). The Hadamard product of A{\rm A} and B{\rm B}, denoted by A∘B{\rm A}\circ{\rm B}, is defined by

A∘B=(ai,j​bi,j)i,j.{\rm A}\circ{\rm B}=\left(a_{i,j}b_{i,j}\right)_{i,j}\,.

We recall some elementary properties of this product. For matrices of Mat⁡(n){\rm Mat}(n), the Hadamard product is commutative, associative, and bilinear. Moreover,

(A∘B)∗=A∗∘B∗,\left({\rm A}\circ{\rm B}\right)^{*}={\rm A}^{*}\circ{\rm B}^{*}\,,

so the Hadamard product of two Hermitian matrices is again Hermitian .

If J{\rm J} denotes the matrix whose entries are all equal to 11, then

A∘J=A,{\rm A}\circ{\rm J}={\rm A}\,,

i.e. J{\rm J} plays the role of the identity matrix for the Hadamard product.

It is known that if A≥0{\rm A}\geq 0 and B≥0{\rm B}\geq 0, then

A∘B≥0.{\rm A}\circ{\rm B}\geq 0\,.

In particular,

A≥0⟹A∘A≥0.{\rm A}\geq 0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad{\rm A}\circ{\rm A}\geq 0\,.

Note that the same conclusion holds if A≤0{\rm A}\leq 0, since

A∘A=(−A)∘(−A)≥0.{\rm A}\circ{\rm A}=\left(-{\rm A}\right)\circ\left(-{\rm A}\right)\geq 0\,.

Similarly, if A≥0{\rm A}\geq 0 and B≤0{\rm B}\leq 0, then A∘B≤0{\rm A}\circ{\rm B}\leq 0 .

The Fréchet derivative ff of a matrix function admits a nice expression in terms of the corresponding Loewner matrix Lf{\rm L}_{f}. The following result is commonly referred to as the Daleckii-Krein formula .

Theorem 2.12.

Let f:(0,∞)→ℝf:\left(0,\infty\right)\to\mathbb{R} be continuously differentiable and let A=diag⁡(λi)∈ℙn{\rm A}={\rm diag}\left(\lambda_{i}\right)\in\mathbb{P}_{n}. Then, for every H∈ℍn{\rm H}\in\mathbb{H}_{n},

D​f​(A)​(H)=Lf​(A)∘H.{\rm D}f({\rm A})({\rm H})={\rm L}_{f}({\rm A})\circ{\rm H}\,.
Remark 2.13.

More generally, if A=U​Δ​U∗{\rm A}={\rm U}\Delta{\rm U}^{*}, with U∈Un{\rm U}\in{\rm U}_{n} and Δ=diag⁡(λi),λi>0\Delta={\rm diag}\left(\lambda_{i}\right),\lambda_{i}>0, then it follows from Lemma 2.7 and Remark 2.10 that

D​f​(A)​(H)=U⁡[Lf​(A)∘(U∗​HU)]​U∗.{\rm D}f({\rm A})({\rm H})={\rm U}\left[{\rm L}_{f}({\rm A})\circ\left({\rm U}^{*}{\rm H}{\rm U}\right)\right]{\rm U}^{*}\,.

Combining the characterization of operator monotonicity given in Proposition 2.6 with Theorem 2.12 and Remark 2.11 gives the following characterization in terms of the Loewner matrix .

Theorem 2.14.

Let I⊆ℝ{\rm I}\subseteq\mathbb{R} be an interval and let f:I⟶ℝf:{\rm I}\longrightarrow\mathbb{R} be continuously differentiable. Then ff is operator monotone increasing if and only if, for every n≥1n\geq 1 and every A∈ℙn{\rm A}\in\mathbb{P}_{n} such that Spec⁡(A)⊆I{\rm Spec}({\rm A})\subseteq{\rm I},

Lf​(A)≥0.{\rm L}_{f}({\rm A})\geq 0\,.

Similarly, ff is operator monotone decreasing if and only if, for every n≥1n\geq 1 and every A∈ℙn{\rm A}\in\mathbb{P}_{n} (with Spec⁡(A)⊆I{\rm Spec}({\rm A})\subseteq{\rm I}),

Lf​(A)≤0.{\rm L}_{f}({\rm A})\leq 0\,.

The previous characterization of operator monotone functions requires the positivity of the Loewner matrix Lf​(A){\rm L}_{f}({\rm A}) for every matrix size n≥1n\geq 1. A natural weaker notion arises by fixing the dimension and requiring the monotonicity condition only for matrices of a given size (introduced in [2]). In particular, we get the following definition.

Definition 2.15.

Let n≥1n\geq 1 and let f:I⟶ℝf:{\rm I}\longrightarrow\mathbb{R} be a function defined on an interval I⊆ℝ{\rm I}\subseteq\mathbb{R}. We say that ff is matrix monotone increasing of degree nn if, for every A,B∈ℍn{\rm A},{\rm B}\in\mathbb{H}_{n} with spectrum contained in I{\rm I},

A≤B⟹f⁡(A)≤f⁡(B).{\rm A}\leq{\rm B}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad f({\rm A})\leq f({\rm B})\,.

Similarly, ff is said to be matrix monotone decreasing of degree nn if

A≤B⟹f⁡(A)≥f⁡(B).{\rm A}\leq{\rm B}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad f({\rm A})\geq f({\rm B})\,.

When no confusion can arise, we say that ff is matrix monotone of degree nn if it is matrix monotone in either of these two directions.

Proposition 2.16.

Let I⊆ℝ{\rm I}\subseteq\mathbb{R} be an interval and let f:I→ℝf:{\rm I}\to\mathbb{R} be matrix monotone of degree nn. Then ff is matrix monotone of degree mm for every 1≤m≤n1\leq m\leq n.

Proof.

Without loss of generality, assume that ff is matrix monotone increasing; otherwise, replace ff by −f-f. Let 1≤m<n1\leq m<n, and let A,B∈ℍm{\rm A},{\rm B}\in\mathbb{H}_{m} have spectra contained in I{\rm I} and satisfy A≤B{\rm A}\leq{\rm B}. Choose α∈I\alpha\in{\rm I}. We denote by A~\widetilde{{\rm A}} and B~\widetilde{{\rm B}} the matrices in Mat⁡(n){\rm Mat}(n) given by

A~:=A⊕α​Idn−m=(A00α​Idn−m),B~:=B⊕α​Idn−m.\widetilde{{\rm A}}:={\rm A}\oplus\alpha{\rm Id}_{n-m}=\begin{pmatrix}{\rm A}&0\\ 0&\alpha{\rm Id}_{n-m}\end{pmatrix}\,,\qquad\widetilde{{\rm B}}:={\rm B}\oplus\alpha{\rm Id}_{n-m}\,.

We have A~,B~∈ℍn\widetilde{{\rm A}}\,,\widetilde{{\rm B}}\in\mathbb{H}_{n} and

B~−A~=(B−A000),\widetilde{{\rm B}}-\widetilde{{\rm A}}=\begin{pmatrix}{\rm B}-{\rm A}&0\\ 0&0\end{pmatrix}\,,

i.e. A~≤B~\widetilde{{\rm A}}\leq\widetilde{{\rm B}}. Since ff is matrix monotone of degree nn, it follows that

f⁡(A~)≤f⁡(B~).f(\widetilde{{\rm A}})\leq f(\widetilde{{\rm B}})\,.

Moreover, it follows from functional calculus that

f⁡(A~)=f⁡(A)⊕f⁡(α)​Idn−m and f⁡(B~)=f⁡(B)⊕f⁡(α)​Idn−m.f(\widetilde{{\rm A}})=f({\rm A})\oplus f(\alpha){\rm Id}_{n-m}\qquad\text{ and }\qquad f(\widetilde{{\rm B}})=f({\rm B})\oplus f(\alpha){\rm Id}_{n-m}\,.

Therefore,

f⁡(A)⊕f⁡(α)​Idn−m≤f⁡(B)⊕f⁡(α)​Idn−m,f({\rm A})\oplus f(\alpha){\rm Id}_{n-m}\leq f({\rm B})\oplus f(\alpha){\rm Id}_{n-m}\,,

which implies

f⁡(A)≤f⁡(B).f({\rm A})\leq f({\rm B})\,.

Hence ff is matrix monotone of degree mm .

∎

Remark 2.17.

We have a natural analogue of Proposition 2.6 and Theorem 2.14 for matrix monotone ff of degree nn. Indeed, a continuously differentiable function f:I→ℝf:{\rm I}\to\mathbb{R} is matrix monotone increasing of degree nn if and only if for every A∈ℙn{\rm A}\in\mathbb{P}_{n} with Spec⁡(A)⊆I{\rm Spec}({\rm A})\subseteq{\rm I}, and every H∈ℍn+{\rm H}\in\mathbb{H}^{+}_{n},

D​f​(A)​(H)≥0.{\rm D}f({\rm A})({\rm H})\geq 0\,.

In particular, ff is matrix monotone increasing of degree nn if and only if Lf​(A)≥0{\rm L}_{f}({\rm A})\geq 0 for all A∈ℙn{\rm A}\in\mathbb{P}_{n} .

However, the previous distinction is genuine: a function may preserve the Loewner order for matrices of degree nn, but not n+1n+1. The following example illustrates this phenomenon and motivates the notion of matrix monotonicity of finite degree (see [6]) .

Example 2.18.

Consider the function

f2​(x)=x+x33.f_{2}(x)=x+\frac{x^{3}}{3}\,.

Since

f2′​(x)=1+x2>0f^{\prime}_{2}(x)=1+x^{2}>0

for every x>0x>0, the function f2f_{2} is strictly increasing, and hence matrix monotone of degree 11 on every interval contained in (0,∞)\left(0\,,\infty\right).

For all D=diag⁡(λ1,λ2){\rm D}={\rm diag}\left(\lambda_{1}\,,\lambda_{2}\right), with λ1≠λ2\lambda_{1}\neq\lambda_{2}, we have

Ω⁡(λ):=f2​(λ1)−f2​(λ2)λ1−λ2=1+λ12+λ1​λ2+λ223.\Omega(\lambda):=\frac{f_{2}(\lambda_{1})-f_{2}(\lambda_{2})}{\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{2}}=1+\frac{\lambda_{1}^{2}+\lambda_{1}\lambda_{2}+\lambda_{2}^{2}}{3}\,.

f2′​(λ1)​f2′​(λ2)−Ω​(λ)2\displaystyle f^{\prime}_{2}(\lambda_{1})f^{\prime}_{2}(\lambda_{2})-\Omega(\lambda)^{2} =\displaystyle= (1+λ12)​(1+λ22)−(1+λ12+λ1​λ2+λ223)2\displaystyle\left(1+\lambda_{1}^{2}\right)\left(1+\lambda_{2}^{2}\right)-\left(1+\frac{\lambda_{1}^{2}+\lambda_{1}\lambda_{2}+\lambda_{2}^{2}}{3}\right)^{2}
=\displaystyle= −(λ1−λ2)2​(λ12+4​λ1​λ2+λ22−3)9.\displaystyle-\frac{\left(\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{2}\right)^{2}\left(\lambda_{1}^{2}+4\lambda_{1}\lambda_{2}+\lambda_{2}^{2}-3\right)}{9}\,.

0<λ1,λ2<12.0<\lambda_{1}\,,\lambda_{2}<\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\,.

Indeed, assume that f2f_{2} is matrix monotone of degree 33 on an interval I{\rm I}. Then for every x∈Ix\in{\rm I}, the associated Hankel matrix

H3​(f2,x):=(f2(i+j−1)​(x)(i+j−1)!)1≤i,j≤3{\rm H}_{3}(f_{2},x):=\left(\frac{f^{(i+j-1)}_{2}(x)}{(i+j-1)!}\right)_{1\leq i,j\leq 3}

must be positive semidefinite. For f2​(x)=x+x33f_{2}(x)=x+\frac{x^{3}}{3}, we have

f2′​(x)=1+x2,f2′′​(x)=2​x,f2′′′​(x)=2,f2(4)​(x)=f2(5)​(x)=0,f^{\prime}_{2}(x)=1+x^{2}\,,\qquad f^{\prime\prime}_{2}(x)=2x\,,\qquad f^{\prime\prime\prime}_{2}(x)=2\,,\qquad f^{(4)}_{2}(x)=f^{(5)}_{2}(x)=0\,,

f3​(x)=x+x33+x55f_{3}(x)=x+\frac{x^{3}}{3}+\frac{x^{5}}{5}

3. Important Examples of Radial Convexity

In this section, we present several examples of metrics on the cone ℙn\mathbb{P}_{n} that are radially convex with respect to the Loewner order, namely the Thompson metric, the standard Riemannian metric, and the Bures-Wasserstein metric. We start with the Thompson metric [13].

Definition 3.1 (Thompson Metric).

Let A,B∈ℙn{\rm A}\,,{\rm B}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}. We define

M⁡(A/B)=inf{α>0,A≤α​B}.{\rm M}({\rm A}/{\rm B})=\inf\left\{\alpha>0\,,{\rm A}\leq\alpha{\rm B}\right\}\,.

The Thompson metric on ℙn\mathbb{P}_{n} is defined by

d∞​(A,B):=log​max⁡{M⁡(A/B),M⁡(B/A)}.{\rm d}_{\infty}({\rm A},{\rm B}):={\rm log}\max\left\{{\rm M}({\rm A}/{\rm B})\,,{\rm M}({\rm B}/{\rm A})\right\}\,.
Remark 3.2.

The Thompson metric is naturally related to the Loewner order. Indeed, for A,B∈ℙn{\rm A},{\rm B}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}, one has

M⁡(A/B)=λmax​(B−12​AB−12).{\rm M}({\rm A}/{\rm B})=\lambda_{\max}\left({\rm B}^{-\frac{1}{2}}{\rm A}{\rm B}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right)\,.

Therefore,

d∞​(A,B)=max⁡{log​λmax​(B−12​AB−12),log​λmax​(A−12​BA−12)}.{\rm d}_{\infty}({\rm A},{\rm B})=\max\left\{{\rm log}\lambda_{\max}\left({\rm B}^{-\frac{1}{2}}{\rm A}{\rm B}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right)\,,{\rm log}\lambda_{\max}\left({\rm A}^{-\frac{1}{2}}{\rm B}{\rm A}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right)\right\}\,.

Equivalently,

d∞​(A,B)=‖log⁡(A−12​BA−12)‖∞,{\rm d}_{\infty}({\rm A},{\rm B})=\left\|{\rm log}\left({\rm A}^{-\frac{1}{2}}{\rm B}{\rm A}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right)\right\|_{\infty}\,,

where ‖⋅‖∞\left\|\cdot\right\|_{\infty} denotes the operator norm. Moreover, d∞{\rm d}_{\infty} satisfies

d∞​(SAS∗,SBS∗)=d∞​(A,B),d∞​(α​A,α​B)=d∞​(A,B),{\rm d}_{\infty}\left({\rm S}{\rm A}{\rm S}^{*},{\rm S}{\rm B}{\rm S}^{*}\right)={\rm d}_{\infty}({\rm A},{\rm B})\,,\qquad{\rm d}_{\infty}(\alpha{\rm A},\alpha{\rm B})={\rm d}_{\infty}({\rm A},{\rm B})\,,

for any invertible matrix S{\rm S} and α>0\alpha>0.

Finally, for r≥0r\geq 0,

d∞​(A,B)≤r if and only if e−r​A≤B≤er​A.{\rm d}_{\infty}({\rm A},{\rm B})\leq r\qquad\text{ if and only if }\qquad e^{-r}{\rm A}\leq{\rm B}\leq e^{r}{\rm A}\,.
Proposition 3.3.

The Thompson metric is radially convex with respect to the Loewner order on ℙn\mathbb{P}_{n} .

Proof.

Let A,B,C∈ℙn{\rm A}\,,{\rm B}\,,{\rm C}\in\mathbb{P}_{n} such that A≤C≤B{\rm A}\leq{\rm C}\leq{\rm B}, and set

r=d∞​(A,B).r={\rm d}_{\infty}({\rm A},{\rm B})\,.

It follows from Remark 3.2 that

e−r​A≤B≤er​A.e^{-r}{\rm A}\leq{\rm B}\leq e^{r}{\rm A}\,.

Since A≤C≤B{\rm A}\leq{\rm C}\leq{\rm B}, we obtain

e−r​A≤A≤C≤B≤er​A.e^{-r}{\rm A}\leq{\rm A}\leq{\rm C}\leq{\rm B}\leq e^{r}{\rm A}\,.

Therefore,

e−r​A≤C≤er​A,e^{-r}{\rm A}\leq{\rm C}\leq e^{r}{\rm A}\,,

and Remark 3.2 implies that

d∞​(A,C)≤r.{\rm d}_{\infty}({\rm A},{\rm C})\leq r\,.

Moreover, since B≤er​A{\rm B}\leq e^{r}{\rm A}, we have

e−r​B≤A≤C.e^{-r}{\rm B}\leq{\rm A}\leq{\rm C}\,.

Together with C≤B{\rm C}\leq{\rm B}, this gives

e−r​B≤C≤B≤er​B.e^{-r}{\rm B}\leq{\rm C}\leq{\rm B}\leq e^{r}{\rm B}\,.

Hence, once again by Remark 3.2,

d∞​(C,B)≤r.{\rm d}_{\infty}({\rm C},{\rm B})\leq r\,.

Finally,

d∞​(A,B)≥max⁡{d∞​(A,C),d∞​(C,B)},{\rm d}_{\infty}({\rm A},{\rm B})\geq\max\left\{{\rm d}_{\infty}({\rm A},{\rm C})\,,{\rm d}_{\infty}({\rm C},{\rm B})\right\}\,,

and the Thompson metric is radially convex with respect to the Loewner order.

∎

Similarly, the standard Riemannian metric on ℙn\mathbb{P}_{n} is radially convex with respect to the Loewner order. We state this result without proof, as it follows from the operator monotonicity of the logarithm and the monotonicity of the Frobenius norm.

Definition 3.4.

Let A,B∈ℙn{\rm A}\,,{\rm B}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}. The standard Riemannian metric on ℙn\mathbb{P}_{n} is defined by

dR​(A,B):=‖log⁡(A−12​BA−12)‖2,{\rm d}_{{\rm R}}({\rm A},{\rm B}):=\left\|{\rm log}\left({\rm A}^{-\frac{1}{2}}{\rm B}{\rm A}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right)\right\|_{2}\,,

where ‖⋅‖2\left\|\cdot\right\|_{2} denotes the Schatten 22-norm (or Frobenius), i.e.

(1) ‖A‖F:=‖A‖2=(tr⁡(A∗​A))12=(∑i,j=1n|ai,j|2)12,(A=(ai,j)∈Mat⁡(n)).\|{\rm A}\|_{{\rm F}}:=\left\|{\rm A}\right\|_{2}=\left({\rm tr}\left({\rm A}^{*}{\rm A}\right)\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}=\left(\sum\limits_{i,j=1}^{n}\left|a_{i,j}\right|^{2}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\,,\qquad\left({\rm A}=\left(a_{i,j}\right)\in{\rm Mat}(n)\right)\,.
Proposition 3.5.

The standard Riemannian metric on ℙn\mathbb{P}_{n} is radially convex with respect to the Loewner order .

From this point on, we write ∥⋅∥F\|\cdot\|_{{\rm F}} for the Frobenius norm, while ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| denotes an arbitrary unitarily invariant norm unless stated otherwise.

Definition 3.6 (Bures-Wasserstein Metric [4]).

Let A,B∈ℙn{\rm A},{\rm B}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}. The Bures-Wasserstein metric on ℙn\mathbb{P}_{n} is defined by

dBW​(A,B):=[tr⁡(A)+tr⁡(B)−2​tr​(A12​BA12)12]12.{\rm d}_{{\rm B}{\rm W}}({\rm A},{\rm B}):=\left[{\rm tr}({\rm A})+{\rm tr}({\rm B})-2{\rm tr}\left({\rm A}^{\frac{1}{2}}{\rm B}{\rm A}^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\right]^{\frac{1}{2}}\,.
Remark 3.7.

We recall some properties of the Bures-Wasserstein metric that will be useful in what follows. First, dBW{\rm d}_{{\rm B}{\rm W}} is symmetric, i.e.

dBW​(A,B)=dBW​(B,A)(A,B∈ℙn).{\rm d}_{{\rm B}{\rm W}}({\rm A},{\rm B})={\rm d}_{{\rm B}{\rm W}}({\rm B},{\rm A})\qquad\left({\rm A}\,,{\rm B}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}\right)\,.

Moreover, the Bures-Wasserstein metric admits the following representation

dBW2​(A,X)=tr⁡(A)+maxY>0⁡(tr⁡[X⁡(Idn−Y−1)−AY]).{\rm d}^{2}_{{\rm B}{\rm W}}({\rm A},{\rm X})={\rm tr}({\rm A})+\max\limits_{{\rm Y}>0}\left({\rm tr}\left[{\rm X}\left({\rm Id}_{n}-{\rm Y}^{-1}\right)-{\rm A}{\rm Y}\right]\right)\,.

For fixed A∈ℙn{\rm A}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}, the maximum is attained at

YX=A−12​(A12​XA12)12​A−12.{\rm Y}_{{\rm X}}={\rm A}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\left({\rm A}^{\frac{1}{2}}{\rm X}{\rm A}^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}{\rm A}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,.

In particular, the operator monotonicity of the square root gives

X≥A⟹YX≥Idn⟹Idn−YX−1≥0,{\rm X}\geq{\rm A}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad{\rm Y}_{{\rm X}}\geq{\rm Id}_{n}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad{\rm Id}_{n}-{\rm Y}^{-1}_{{\rm X}}\geq 0\,,

while

X≤A⟹YX≤Idn⟹Idn−YX−1≤0.{\rm X}\leq{\rm A}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad{\rm Y}_{{\rm X}}\leq{\rm Id}_{n}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad{\rm Id}_{n}-{\rm Y}^{-1}_{{\rm X}}\leq 0\,.
Proposition 3.8.

The Bures-Wasserstein metric on ℙn\mathbb{P}_{n} is radially convex with respect to the Loewner order .

Proof.

Let A,B,C∈ℙn{\rm A},{\rm B},{\rm C}\in\mathbb{P}_{n} such that A≤C≤B{\rm A}\leq{\rm C}\leq{\rm B}. To simplify the notation, for fixed Ω∈ℙn\Omega\in\mathbb{P}_{n}, define

gΩ​(X):=maxY>0⁡(tr⁡[X⁡(Idn−Y−1)−Ω​Y]).g_{\Omega}({\rm X}):=\max_{{\rm Y}>0}\left({\rm tr}\left[{\rm X}\left({\rm Id}_{n}-{\rm Y}^{-1}\right)-\Omega{\rm Y}\right]\right)\,.

In particular, it follows from Remark 3.7 that

dBW2​(A,X)=tr⁡(A)+gA​(X).{\rm d}_{{\rm B}{\rm W}}^{2}({\rm A},{\rm X})={\rm tr}({\rm A})+g_{{\rm A}}({\rm X})\,.

Let YC{\rm Y}_{{\rm C}} denote the maximizer in the definition of gA​(C)g_{{\rm A}}({\rm C}). Since C≥A{\rm C}\geq{\rm A}, Remark 3.7 gives

YC≥Idn,{\rm Y}_{{\rm C}}\geq{\rm Id}_{n}\,,

and hence

Idn−YC−1≥0.{\rm Id}_{n}-{\rm Y}^{-1}_{{\rm C}}\geq 0\,.

Since B≥C{\rm B}\geq{\rm C}, it follows that

tr⁡[B⁡(Idn−YC−1)]≥tr⁡[C⁡(Idn−YC−1)].{\rm tr}\left[{\rm B}\left({\rm Id}_{n}-{\rm Y}_{{\rm C}}^{-1}\right)\right]\geq{\rm tr}\left[{\rm C}\left({\rm Id}_{n}-{\rm Y}_{{\rm C}}^{-1}\right)\right]\,.

Hence,

gA​(B)≥tr⁡[B⁡(Idn−YC−1)−AYC]≥tr⁡[C⁡(Idn−YC−1)−AYC]=gA​(C).g_{{\rm A}}({\rm B})\geq{\rm tr}\left[{\rm B}\left({\rm Id}_{n}-{\rm Y}_{{\rm C}}^{-1}\right)-{\rm A}{\rm Y}_{{\rm C}}\right]\geq{\rm tr}\left[{\rm C}\left({\rm Id}_{n}-{\rm Y}^{-1}_{{\rm C}}\right)-{\rm A}{\rm Y}_{{\rm C}}\right]=g_{{\rm A}}({\rm C})\,.

Thus

dBW2​(A,C)≤dBW2​(A,B),{\rm d}^{2}_{{\rm B}{\rm W}}({\rm A},{\rm C})\leq{\rm d}^{2}_{{\rm B}{\rm W}}({\rm A},{\rm B})\,,

which implies

dBW​(A,C)≤dBW​(A,B).{\rm d}_{{\rm B}{\rm W}}({\rm A},{\rm C})\leq{\rm d}_{{\rm B}{\rm W}}({\rm A},{\rm B})\,.

Similarly, using the same argument with B{\rm B} fixed and the fact that A≤C≤B{\rm A}\leq{\rm C}\leq{\rm B}, we obtain

dBW​(C,B)≤dBW​(A,B).{\rm d}_{{\rm B}{\rm W}}({\rm C},{\rm B})\leq{\rm d}_{{\rm B}{\rm W}}({\rm A},{\rm B})\,.

Finally,

dBW​(A,B)≥max⁡{dBW​(A,C),dBW​(C,B)}.{\rm d}_{{\rm B}{\rm W}}({\rm A},{\rm B})\geq\max\left\{{\rm d}_{{\rm B}{\rm W}}({\rm A},{\rm C})\,,{\rm d}_{{\rm B}{\rm W}}({\rm C},{\rm B})\right\}\,.

∎

The last example in this section, is the most important one for the objectives of this article. We now focus on the ff-metric induced by a function f:(0,∞)→(0,∞)f:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty) and a norm ∥⋅∥,\|\cdot\|,

d∥⋅∥,f(A,B):=‖f(A)−f(B)‖.{\rm d}_{\|\cdot\|,f}({\rm A},{\rm B}):=\left\|f({\rm A})-f({\rm B})\right\|\,.
Proposition 3.9.

Let f:(0,∞)→ℝf:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R} be matrix monotone of degree nn, and let ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| be a monotone norm on ℙn\mathbb{P}_{n}. Then d∥⋅∥,f{\rm d}_{\|\cdot\|,f} is radially convex of order nn with respect to the Loewner order on ℙn\mathbb{P}_{n}.

Proof.

Let A,B,C∈ℙn{\rm A},{\rm B}\,,{\rm C}\in\mathbb{P}_{n} such that A≤C≤B{\rm A}\leq{\rm C}\leq{\rm B}. Without loss of generality, we assume that ff is matrix monotone increasing of degree nn; otherwise, replace ff by −f-f. Hence,

0≤f⁡(C)−f⁡(A)≤f⁡(B)−f⁡(A).0\leq f({\rm C})-f({\rm A})\leq f({\rm B})-f({\rm A})\,.

Since ‖⋅‖\left\|\cdot\right\| is monotone,

d‖⋅‖,f​(A,C)=‖f⁡(C)−f⁡(A)‖≤‖f⁡(B)−f⁡(A)‖=d‖⋅‖,f​(A,B).{\rm d}_{\left\|\cdot\right\|,f}({\rm A},{\rm C})=\left\|f({\rm C})-f({\rm A})\right\|\leq\left\|f({\rm B})-f({\rm A})\right\|={\rm d}_{\left\|\cdot\right\|,f}({\rm A},{\rm B})\,.

Similarly,

d‖⋅‖,f​(C,B)=‖f⁡(B)−f⁡(C)‖≤‖f⁡(B)−f⁡(A)‖=d‖⋅‖,f​(A,B).{\rm d}_{\left\|\cdot\right\|,f}({\rm C},{\rm B})=\left\|f({\rm B})-f({\rm C})\right\|\leq\left\|f({\rm B})-f({\rm A})\right\|={\rm d}_{\left\|\cdot\right\|,f}({\rm A},{\rm B})\,.

Therefore

d‖⋅‖,f​(A,B)≥max⁡{d‖⋅‖,f​(A,C),d‖⋅‖,f​(C,B)},{\rm d}_{\left\|\cdot\right\|,f}({\rm A},{\rm B})\geq\max\left\{{\rm d}_{\left\|\cdot\right\|,f}({\rm A},{\rm C})\,,{\rm d}_{\left\|\cdot\right\|,f}({\rm C},{\rm B})\right\}\,,

and d∥⋅∥,f{\rm d}_{\|\cdot\|,f} is radially convex of order nn with respect to the Loewner order.

∎

4. Frobenius norm: From Radial Convexity to Monotonicity

In this section, we focus on radial convexity with respect to the Frobenius norm and investigate the converse direction of the last result obtained in the previous section. We first derive a necessary differential condition for radial convexity and then characterize this condition in terms of the positivity of the Hadamard square of the corresponding Loewner matrix. This leads naturally to the question of whether radial convexity of order nn implies matrix monotonicity of the same degree. We formulate this question as a conjecture, prove it in degree 22, and conclude with examples supporting the conjecture in higher degrees.

Recall that, since the Frobenius norm is fixed throughout this section, we say that ff is radially convex of order nn if the metric df{\rm d}_{f} induced by ff is radially convex with respect to the Loewner order on ℙn\mathbb{P}_{n}. We start with a proposition .

Proposition 4.1.

Let f:(0,∞)→ℝf:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R} be continuous. If ff is radially convex of order nn, then ff is monotone of degree 11 on (0,∞)(0,\infty) .

Remark 4.2.

We recall a classical result. Let x,y,z∈ℝx\,,y\,,z\in\mathbb{R}. Suppose that

|x−z|≤|x−y| and |z−y|≤|x−y|.\left|x-z\right|\leq\left|x-y\right|\qquad\text{ and }\qquad\left|z-y\right|\leq\left|x-y\right|\,.

Then zz lies between xx and yy. In other words, we have

min⁡{x,y}≤z≤max⁡{x,y}.\min\left\{x\,,y\right\}\leq z\leq\max\left\{x\,,y\right\}\,.
Proof of Proposition 4.1.

Let 0<a<c<b0<a<c<b. Let A,B,C{\rm A},{\rm B},{\rm C} be the matrices given by

A=a​Idn,C=c​Idn,B=b​Idn.{\rm A}=a{\rm Id}_{n}\,,\qquad{\rm C}=c{\rm Id}_{n}\,,\qquad{\rm B}=b{\rm Id}_{n}\,.

Then A≤C≤B{\rm A}\leq{\rm C}\leq{\rm B}. By the radial convexity hypothesis, we get

d⁡(A,C)≤d⁡(A,B) and d⁡(C,B)≤d⁡(A,B).{\rm d}({\rm A},{\rm C})\leq{\rm d}({\rm A},{\rm B})\qquad\text{ and }\qquad{\rm d}({\rm C},{\rm B})\leq{\rm d}({\rm A},{\rm B})\,.

Since

f⁡(a​Idn)=f⁡(a)​Idn,f⁡(c​Idn)=f⁡(c)​Idn,f⁡(b​Idn)=f⁡(b)​Idn,f(a{\rm Id}_{n})=f(a){\rm Id}_{n}\,,\qquad f(c{\rm Id}_{n})=f(c){\rm Id}_{n}\,,\qquad f(b{\rm Id}_{n})=f(b){\rm Id}_{n}\,,

we have

d⁡(A,C)=|f⁡(a)−f⁡(c)|​‖Idn‖ and d⁡(A,B)=|f⁡(a)−f⁡(b)|​‖Idn‖.{\rm d}({\rm A},{\rm C})=\left|f(a)-f(c)\right|\left\|{\rm Id}_{n}\right\|\qquad\text{ and }\qquad{\rm d}({\rm A},{\rm B})=\left|f(a)-f(b)\right|\left\|{\rm Id}_{n}\right\|\,.

|f⁡(a)−f⁡(c)|≤|f⁡(a)−f⁡(b)| and |f⁡(c)−f⁡(b)|≤|f⁡(a)−f⁡(b)|.\left|f(a)-f(c)\right|\leq\left|f(a)-f(b)\right|\qquad\text{ and }\qquad\left|f(c)-f(b)\right|\leq\left|f(a)-f(b)\right|\,.

We now prove an analogue of Proposition 2.16

Proposition 4.3.

Let f:(0,∞)→ℝf:\left(0,\infty\right)\to\mathbb{R}. If ff is radially convex of order nn with respect to d:=df{\rm d}:={\rm d}_{f}, then it is radially convex of order mm for every 1≤m≤n1\leq m\leq n .

Remark 4.4.

Using the embedding Mat⁡(m)↪Mat⁡(n),1≤m≤n{\rm Mat}(m)\hookrightarrow{\rm Mat}(n)\,,1\leq m\leq n, we get, for all X∈ℍm{\rm X}\in\mathbb{H}_{m}, that

(2) ‖X⊕0n−m‖=‖X‖.\left\|{\rm X}\oplus 0_{n-m}\right\|=\left\|{\rm X}\right\|\,.

This is not specific to the Frobenius norm; the same result remains valid for any unitarily invariant norm .

Proof.

Let 1≤m<n1\leq m<n, and let A,B,C∈ℙm{\rm A},{\rm B},{\rm C}\in\mathbb{P}_{m} such that A≤C≤B{\rm A}\leq{\rm C}\leq{\rm B}. Let α>0\alpha>0, and let

A~:=A⊕α​Idn−m,C~:=C⊕α​Idn−m,B~:=B⊕α​Idn−m.\widetilde{{\rm A}}:={\rm A}\oplus\alpha{\rm Id}_{n-m}\,,\qquad\widetilde{{\rm C}}:={\rm C}\oplus\alpha{\rm Id}_{n-m}\,,\qquad\widetilde{{\rm B}}:={\rm B}\oplus\alpha{\rm Id}_{n-m}\,.

In particular, A~≤C~≤B~\widetilde{{\rm A}}\leq\widetilde{{\rm C}}\leq\widetilde{{\rm B}}. By radial convexity of order nn, we get

d⁡(A~,C~)≤d⁡(A~,B~) and d⁡(C~,B~)≤d⁡(A~,B~).{\rm d}\left(\widetilde{{\rm A}},\widetilde{{\rm C}}\right)\leq{\rm d}\left(\widetilde{{\rm A}},\widetilde{{\rm B}}\right)\qquad\text{ and }\qquad{\rm d}\left(\widetilde{{\rm C}},\widetilde{{\rm B}}\right)\leq{\rm d}\left(\widetilde{{\rm A}},\widetilde{{\rm B}}\right)\,.

Again, by functional calculus, we get

f⁡(A~)−f⁡(C~)=(f⁡(A)−f⁡(C))⊕0n−m,f⁡(A~)−f⁡(B~)=(f⁡(A)−f⁡(B))⊕0n−m,f(\widetilde{{\rm A}})-f(\widetilde{{\rm C}})=\left(f({\rm A})-f({\rm C})\right)\oplus 0_{n-m}\,,\qquad f(\widetilde{{\rm A}})-f(\widetilde{{\rm B}})=\left(f({\rm A})-f({\rm B})\right)\oplus 0_{n-m}\,,

and

f⁡(C~)−f⁡(B~)=(f⁡(C)−f⁡(B))⊕0n−m.f(\widetilde{{\rm C}})-f(\widetilde{{\rm B}})=\left(f({\rm C})-f({\rm B})\right)\oplus 0_{n-m}\,.

Using the compatibility of the norm with block embeddings (see Remark 4.4), we obtain

‖f⁡(A)−f⁡(C)‖=d⁡(A,C)≤d⁡(A,B)=‖f⁡(A)−f⁡(B)‖\left\|f({\rm A})-f({\rm C})\right\|={\rm d}({\rm A},{\rm C})\leq{\rm d}({\rm A},{\rm B})=\left\|f({\rm A})-f({\rm B})\right\|

and

‖f⁡(B)−f⁡(C)‖=d⁡(B,C)≤d⁡(A,B)=‖f⁡(A)−f⁡(B)‖.\left\|f({\rm B})-f({\rm C})\right\|={\rm d}({\rm B},{\rm C})\leq{\rm d}({\rm A},{\rm B})=\left\|f({\rm A})-f({\rm B})\right\|\,.

Thus ff is radially convex of order mm.

Let f:(0,∞)→ℝf:\left(0\,,\infty\right)\to\mathbb{R} be differentiable, and assume that ff is radially convex of order nn. Then, for every A∈ℙn{\rm A}\in\mathbb{P}_{n} and every X,Y≥0{\rm X}\,,{\rm Y}\geq 0, we have

=‖D​f​(A)​(X)‖F2+2​s​Re​⟨D​f​(A)​(X),D​f​(A)​(Y)⟩F+s2​‖D​f​(A)​(Y)‖F2.=\left\|{\rm D}f({\rm A})({\rm X})\right\|^{2}_{{\rm F}}+2s{\rm Re}\langle{\rm D}f({\rm A})({\rm X})\,,{\rm D}f({\rm A})({\rm Y})\rangle_{{\rm F}}+s^{2}\left\|{\rm D}f({\rm A})({\rm Y})\right\|^{2}_{{\rm F}}\,.

The preceding results motivate the following conjecture, which connects radial convexity with matrix monotonicity at each finite order.

Conjecture 4.10.

Let f:(0,∞)→ℝf:\left(0,\infty\right)\to\mathbb{R}. Then ff is radially convex of order nn (with respect to the Frobenius norm) if and only if ff is matrix monotone of degree nn .

By Proposition 3.9, matrix monotonicity of degree nn implies radial convexity of order nn. Thus, it remains to prove the converse implication. The next theorem establishes the conjecture for n=2n=2.

Theorem 4.11.

Let f:(0,∞)→ℝf:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R} be differentiable and radially convex of order 22. Then ff is matrix monotone of degree 22. In other words, Conjecture 4.10 holds for n=2n=2 .

Proof.

We argue by contraposition. By Proposition 4.1, radial convexity of order 22 implies that ff is monotone on (0,∞)(0,\infty). Suppose that ff is not matrix monotone of degree 22. Then there exist λ1,λ2>0\lambda_{1}\,,\lambda_{2}>0, with λ1≠λ2\lambda_{1}\neq\lambda_{2}, such that

a​b−Ω2<0,ab-\Omega^{2}<0\,,

with a:=f′​(λ1),b:=f′​(λ2),a:=f^{\prime}\left(\lambda_{1}\right)\,,b:=f^{\prime}\left(\lambda_{2}\right)\,, and Ω:=f⁡(λ1)−f⁡(λ2)λ1−λ2\Omega:=\frac{f\left(\lambda_{1}\right)-f\left(\lambda_{2}\right)}{\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{2}}.

Since ff is monotone, aa and bb have the same sign, and therefore a​b≥0ab\geq 0. Let

A=(λ100λ2) and L:=Lf​(diag⁡(λ1,λ2))=(aΩΩb).{\rm A}=\begin{pmatrix}\lambda_{1}&0\\ 0&\lambda_{2}\end{pmatrix}\quad\text{ and }\quad{\rm L}:={\rm L}_{f}\left({\rm diag}(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2})\right)=\begin{pmatrix}a&\Omega\\ \Omega&b\end{pmatrix}\,.

Recall that for every Hermitian matrix H{\rm H}, we have

D​f​(A)​(H)=L∘H.{\rm D}f({\rm A})({\rm H})={\rm L}\circ{\rm H}\,.

In particular,

L∘L=(a2Ω2Ω2b2),{\rm L}\circ{\rm L}=\begin{pmatrix}a^{2}&\Omega^{2}\\ \Omega^{2}&b^{2}\end{pmatrix}\,,

so

det(L∘L)=a2​b2−Ω4=(a​b−Ω2)​(a​b+Ω2)<0.\det\left({\rm L}\circ{\rm L}\right)=a^{2}b^{2}-\Omega^{4}=\left(ab-\Omega^{2}\right)\left(ab+\Omega^{2}\right)<0\,.

Hence L∘L{\rm L}\circ{\rm L} is indefinite. Therefore, there exists a vector v=(v1v2)∈ℝ2v=\begin{pmatrix}v_{1}\\ v_{2}\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{2} such that

vt​(L∘L)​v<0.v^{t}\left({\rm L}\circ{\rm L}\right)v<0\,.

Let u=(u1u2)∈ℝ2u=\begin{pmatrix}u_{1}\\ u_{2}\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{2} and let

U:=u​ut=(u12u1​u2u1​u2u22),V:=v​vt=(v12v1​v2v1​v2v22).{\rm U}:=uu^{t}=\begin{pmatrix}u^{2}_{1}&u_{1}u_{2}\\ u_{1}u_{2}&u^{2}_{2}\end{pmatrix}\,,\qquad{\rm V}:=vv^{t}=\begin{pmatrix}v^{2}_{1}&v_{1}v_{2}\\ v_{1}v_{2}&v^{2}_{2}\end{pmatrix}\,.

Clearly, U,V≥0{\rm U}\,,{\rm V}\geq 0 (determinant is 00, and hermitian because the coefficients are real). Since

D​f​(A)​(U)=L∘U and D​f​(A)​(V)=L∘V,{\rm D}f({\rm A})({\rm U})={\rm L}\circ{\rm U}\quad\text{ and }\quad{\rm D}f({\rm A})({\rm V})={\rm L}\circ{\rm V}\,,

we obtain

⟨D​f​(A)​(U),D​f​(A)​(V)⟩F=∑i,j=12Li​j2​ui​uj​vi​vj=(u∘v)t​(L∘L)​(u∘v).\langle{\rm D}f({\rm A})({\rm U})\,,{\rm D}f({\rm A})({\rm V})\rangle_{{\rm F}}=\sum\limits_{i,j=1}^{2}{\rm L}^{2}_{ij}u_{i}u_{j}v_{i}v_{j}=\left(u\circ v\right)^{t}\left({\rm L}\circ{\rm L}\right)\left(u\circ v\right)\,.

Take u1=u2=1u_{1}=u_{2}=1, i.e.

U=(1111) and u∘v=v.{\rm U}=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\ 1&1\end{pmatrix}\quad\text{ and }\quad u\circ v=v\,.

so it follows that

⟨D​f​(A)​(U),D​f​(A)​(V)⟩F=vt​(L∘L)​v<0.\langle{\rm D}f({\rm A})({\rm U})\,,{\rm D}f({\rm A})({\rm V})\rangle_{{\rm F}}=v^{t}\left({\rm L}\circ{\rm L}\right)v<0\,.

In particular, it follows that ff is not radially convex of order 22 (see Proposition 4.5), contradicting our initial hypothesis on ff. Therefore ff is matrix monotone of degree 22.

Remark 4.12.

The proof of the conjecture for n=2n=2 relies strongly on the particular form of the determinant of a 2×22\times 2 matrix. Indeed, if

L=(abbc),{\rm L}=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\ b&c\end{pmatrix}\,,

then

det(L∘L)=a2​c2−b4=(a​c−b2)​(a​c+b2)=det(L)​(a​c+b2).\det({\rm L}\circ{\rm L})=a^{2}c^{2}-b^{4}=\left(ac-b^{2}\right)\left(ac+b^{2}\right)=\det({\rm L})\left(ac+b^{2}\right)\,.

Therefore, once the signs of the diagonal entries are known, the positive semidefiniteness of L∘L{\rm L}\circ{\rm L} provides direct information about the sign of det(L)\det({\rm L}). This is the key observation used in the proof of the conjecture in degree 22.

The situation becomes considerably more subtle in degree 33. Let

L=(axyxbzyzc).{\rm L}=\begin{pmatrix}a&x&y\\ x&b&z\\ y&z&c\end{pmatrix}\,.

A direct computation gives

det(L)=a​b​c+2​x​y​z−a​z2−b​y2−c​x2,\det({\rm L})=abc+2xyz-az^{2}-by^{2}-cx^{2}\,,

whereas

det(L∘L)=a2​b2​c2+2​x2​y2​z2−a2​z4−b2​y4−c2​x4.\det({\rm L}\circ{\rm L})=a^{2}b^{2}c^{2}+2x^{2}y^{2}z^{2}-a^{2}z^{4}-b^{2}y^{4}-c^{2}x^{4}\,.

In contrast with the 2×22\times 2 case, there is no analogous factorization involving det(L)\det({\rm L}). More importantly, the Hadamard square loses information concerning the signs of the off-diagonal entries. In particular, the term 2​x​y​z2xyz appearing in det(L)\det({\rm L}) is replaced by 2​x2​y2​z22x^{2}y^{2}z^{2} in det(L∘L)\det({\rm L}\circ{\rm L}). Thus, the positivity of L∘L{\rm L}\circ{\rm L} does not, for a general symmetric matrix, determine the sign of det(L)\det({\rm L}).

Remark 4.13.

Suppose that ff is radially convex of order nn. Then, by Propositions 4.5 and 4.8, for every diagonal matrix A∈ℙn{\rm A}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}, we have Lf​(A)∘Lf​(A)≥0{\rm L}_{f}({\rm A})\circ{\rm L}_{f}({\rm A})\geq 0. Let 1≤m≤n1\leq m\leq n and let B=diag⁡(λ1,…,λm)∈ℙm{\rm B}={\rm diag}\left(\lambda_{1}\,,\ldots\,,\lambda_{m}\right)\in\mathbb{P}_{m}. Choose λm+1,…,λn>0\lambda_{m+1},\ldots,\lambda_{n}>0 and consider A=diag​(λi)1≤i≤n∈ℙn{\rm A}={\rm diag}\left(\lambda_{i}\right)_{1\leq i\leq n}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}. By construction, Lf​(B){\rm L}_{f}({\rm B}) is the leading principal submatrix of size mm of Lf​(A){\rm L}_{f}({\rm A}). Therefore, Lf​(B)∘Lf​(B){\rm L}_{f}({\rm B})\circ{\rm L}_{f}({\rm B}) is the corresponding principal submatrix of Lf​(A)∘Lf​(A){\rm L}_{f}({\rm A})\circ{\rm L}_{f}({\rm A}). Since every principal submatrix of a positive semidefinite matrix is positive semidefinite, we obtain

Lf​(B)∘Lf​(B)≥0.{\rm L}_{f}({\rm B})\circ{\rm L}_{f}({\rm B})\geq 0\,.

However, this argument alone does not imply that ff is radially convex of order mm, since the positivity of Lf​(B)∘Lf​(B){\rm L}_{f}({\rm B})\circ{\rm L}_{f}({\rm B}) has only been shown to be a necessary condition for radial convexity. This provides a weaker version of Proposition 4.3, but shows directly how the corresponding Loewner matrices behave when passing to a lower degree.

The previous remark shows that the argument used for n=2n=2 does not extend directly to n=3n=3. Nevertheless, radial convexity already provides most of the inequalities required for the positivity of the corresponding Loewner matrix. More precisely, we have the following result.

Proposition 4.14.

Let f:(0,∞)→ℝf:\left(0,\infty\right)\to\mathbb{R} be differentiable and increasing, and assume that ff is radially convex of order 33. Then ff is matrix monotone of degree 33 if and only if

det(Lf​(A))≥0\det\left({\rm L}_{f}({\rm A})\right)\geq 0

for every A∈ℙ3{\rm A}\in\mathbb{P}_{3} .

Remark 4.15.

Recall that a Hermitian matrix is positive semidefinite if and only if all of its principal minors are nonnegative. More precisely, if

A=(axyx¯bzy¯z¯c)∈ℍ3,{\rm A}=\begin{pmatrix}a&x&y\\ \overline{x}&b&z\\ \overline{y}&\overline{z}&c\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{H}_{3}\,,

then its principal minors of order 11 are

a,b,c,a\,,\qquad b\,,\qquad c\,,

its principal minors of order 22 are

a​b−|x|2,a​c−|y|2,b​c−|z|2,ab-\left|x\right|^{2}\,,\qquad ac-\left|y\right|^{2}\,,\qquad bc-\left|z\right|^{2}\,,

and its unique principal minor of order 33 is det(A)\det({\rm A}). In particular, A≥0{\rm A}\geq 0 if and only if all seven of these quantities are nonnegative.

Proof.

The direct implication follows immediately from Remark 2.17. Assume that det(Lf​(A))≥0\det\left({\rm L}_{f}({\rm A})\right)\geq 0 for every A∈ℙ3{\rm A}\in\mathbb{P}_{3}. The goal is to show that ff is matrix monotone of degree 33.

Lf​(D)=(a1xyxa2zyza3){\rm L}_{f}({\rm D})=\begin{pmatrix}a_{1}&x&y\\ x&a_{2}&z\\ y&z&a_{3}\end{pmatrix}

be the corresponding Loewner matrix (with ai=f′​(λi),1≤i≤3a_{i}=f^{\prime}(\lambda_{i}),1\leq i\leq 3). Since ff is increasing,

f′​(λi)≥0,(1≤i≤3),f^{\prime}(\lambda_{i})\geq 0\,,\qquad\left(1\leq i\leq 3\right)\,,

i.e. all the principal minors of order 11 of Lf​(D){\rm L}_{f}({\rm D}) are nonnegative.

On the other hand, since ff is radially convex of order 33, it follows from Propositions 4.5 and 4.8 that

Lf​(D)∘Lf​(D)=(a12x2y2x2a22z2y2z2a32)≥0.{\rm L}_{f}({\rm D})\circ{\rm L}_{f}({\rm D})=\begin{pmatrix}a_{1}^{2}&x^{2}&y^{2}\\ x^{2}&a_{2}^{2}&z^{2}\\ y^{2}&z^{2}&a_{3}^{2}\end{pmatrix}\geq 0.

Therefore, all of its principal minors of order 22 are nonnegative, and hence

a12​a22−x4≥0,a12​a32−y4≥0,a22​a32−z4≥0.a_{1}^{2}a_{2}^{2}-x^{4}\geq 0,\qquad a_{1}^{2}a_{3}^{2}-y^{4}\geq 0,\qquad a_{2}^{2}a_{3}^{2}-z^{4}\geq 0.

Since

a12​a22−x4=(a1​a2−x2)​(a1​a2+x2)a^{2}_{1}a^{2}_{2}-x^{4}=\left(a_{1}a_{2}-x^{2}\right)\left(a_{1}a_{2}+x^{2}\right)

and a1,a2≥0a_{1},a_{2}\geq 0, it follows that a1​a2−x2≥0a_{1}a_{2}-x^{2}\geq 0. Similarly,

Thus, all the principal minors of order 22 of Lf​(D){\rm L}_{f}({\rm D}) are nonnegative.

Finally, by assumption,

det(Lf​(D))≥0.\det\left({\rm L}_{f}({\rm D})\right)\geq 0\,.

Hence all the principal minors of Lf​(D){\rm L}_{f}({\rm D}) are nonnegative. It follows from Remark 4.15 that Lf​(D)≥0{\rm L}_{f}({\rm D})\geq 0. Since D∈ℙ3{\rm D}\in\mathbb{P}_{3} was arbitrary, the Loewner characterization implies that ff is matrix monotone of degree 33.

5. Concluding remarks and future directions

The main purpose of this paper was to investigate the relationship between matrix monotonicity and radial convexity on the cone of positive definite matrices. In Section 3, we showed that matrix monotonicity implies radial convexity for a large family of metrics. In particular, this is the case for metrics of the form

d‖⋅‖,f​(A,B)=‖f⁡(A)−f⁡(B)‖,{\rm d}_{\left\|\cdot\right\|,f}({\rm A},{\rm B})=\left\|f({\rm A})-f({\rm B})\right\|\,,

where ‖⋅‖\left\|\cdot\right\| is a unitarily invariant norm and ff is an appropriate matrix monotone function. We also established radial convexity for several other natural metrics on the cone of positive definite matrices.

In Section 4, we considered the converse problem for the metric induced by the Frobenius norm. This led us to conjecture that, for every n≥1n\geq 1, radial convexity of order nn is equivalent to matrix monotonicity of degree nn. We proved this conjecture for n=2n=2. More generally, we showed that radial convexity imposes a positivity condition on the Hadamard square of the corresponding Loewner matrix, providing a direct link between the metric geometry of the positive definite cone and the classical Loewner characterization of matrix monotonicity.

These results suggest several directions for future work. A first natural problem is to investigate the converse implication for arbitrary unitarily invariant norms. More precisely, given a unitarily invariant norm ‖⋅‖\left\|\cdot\right\|, one may ask whether radial convexity with respect to d∥⋅∥,f{\rm d}_{\|\cdot\|,f} characterizes matrix monotonicity of ff at each finite degree. In the case of the Frobenius norm, the differential characterization obtained in Section 4 leads to a condition involving the Hadamard square of the Loewner matrix. It would be interesting to determine the corresponding infinitesimal condition for other unitarily invariant norms and to obtain an analogue of the implications established in that section.

A second direction is to move beyond metrics induced by unitarily invariant norms and investigate similar phenomena for other natural geometries on the positive definite cone. The broader objective is to develop alternative geometric and metric characterizations of matrix monotonicity. In particular, finite-degree matrix monotonicity exhibits a subtle dependence on the matrix size: a function may be matrix monotone of degree nn but fail to be matrix monotone of degree n+1n+1. Understanding radial convexity for different metrics may provide new ways to identify the mechanisms responsible for this loss of monotonicity and, more generally, to better understand the distinction between the different degrees of matrix monotonicity.

Returning to the first direction, we conclude by showing that the equivalence obtained in degree 22 for the Frobenius norm extends, under a mild non-degeneracy assumption, to every unitarily invariant norm. In Theorem 5.4, we show that this additional assumption can in fact be removed.

Proposition 5.1.

Let f:(0,∞)→(0,∞)f:\left(0,\infty\right)\to\left(0,\infty\right) be differentiable and increasing, and let ‖⋅‖\left\|\cdot\right\| be a unitarily invariant norm. Assume that ff is not matrix monotone of degree 22. Suppose moreover that there exist a≠ba\neq b such that Lf​(a,b){\rm L}_{f}(a,b) is not positive semidefinite and

f′​(a)​f′​(b)>0.f^{\prime}(a)f^{\prime}(b)>0\,.

Then there exist A,B,C∈ℙ2{\rm A},{\rm B},{\rm C}\in\mathbb{P}_{2} such that

A≤C≤B and ‖f⁡(A)−f⁡(C)‖>‖f⁡(A)−f⁡(B)‖.{\rm A}\leq{\rm C}\leq{\rm B}\qquad\text{ and }\qquad\left\|f({\rm A})-f({\rm C})\right\|>\left\|f({\rm A})-f({\rm B})\right\|\,.

Remark 5.3.

An analogous result holds when ff is differentiable and decreasing; the proof is similar.

Theorem 5.4.

Let f:(0,∞)→ℝf:\left(0,\infty\right)\to\mathbb{R} be differentiable, and let ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| be a unitarily invariant norm. Then ff is radially convex of order 22 with respect to the metric d∥⋅∥,f{\rm d}_{\|\cdot\|,f} if and only if ff is matrix monotone of degree 22.

Proof.

If ff is matrix monotone of degree 22, then Proposition 3.9 shows that ff is radially convex of order 22 with respect to d∥⋅∥,f{\rm d}_{\|\cdot\|,f}.

For the converse, we argue by contraposition. In view of the preceding proposition, it is enough to show that the additional assumption

f′​(a)​f′​(b)>0f^{\prime}(a)f^{\prime}(b)>0

can always be satisfied. Suppose that ff is not matrix monotone of degree 22. If ff is not monotone on (0,∞)\left(0,\infty\right), then Proposition 4.1 implies that ff is not radially convex of order 22, and there is nothing to prove. We may therefore assume that ff is monotone. Without loss of generality, we may assume that ff is increasing; otherwise, replace ff by −f-f, which induces the same metric. Then there exist a<ba<b such that

Lf​(a,b)=(f′​(a)f[1]​(a,b)f[1]​(a,b)f′​(b)){\rm L}_{f}(a,b)=\begin{pmatrix}f^{\prime}(a)&f^{[1]}(a,b)\\ f^{[1]}(a,b)&f^{\prime}(b)\end{pmatrix}

is not positive semidefinite. Since ff is increasing,

f′​(a)≥0,f′​(b)≥0,f[1]​(a,b)≥0.f^{\prime}(a)\geq 0\,,\qquad f^{\prime}(b)\geq 0\,,\qquad f^{[1]}(a,b)\geq 0\,.

Hence

f′​(a)​f′​(b)−f[1]​(a,b)2<0.f^{\prime}(a)f^{\prime}(b)-f^{[1]}(a,b)^{2}<0\,.

In particular, f[1]​(a,b)>0f^{[1]}(a,b)>0.

If f′​(a)>0f^{\prime}(a)>0 and f′​(b)>0f^{\prime}(b)>0, then the hypotheses of the preceding proposition are satisfied, and the result follows. It remains to consider the case in which at least one of f′​(a)f^{\prime}(a) and f′​(b)f^{\prime}(b) is zero. Suppose first that f′​(a)=0f^{\prime}(a)=0 and f′​(b)>0f^{\prime}(b)>0. By the mean value theorem, there exists c∈(a,b)c\in\left(a,b\right) such that

f′​(c)=f[1]​(a,b)>0.f^{\prime}(c)=f^{[1]}(a,b)>0\,.

By Darboux’s theorem for derivatives, for every sufficiently small ε>0\varepsilon>0 there exists aε∈(a,c)a_{\varepsilon}\in\left(a,c\right) such that

f′​(aε)=ε.f^{\prime}(a_{\varepsilon})=\varepsilon.

Since f′​(c)>0f^{\prime}(c)>0 and ff is increasing, we have f⁡(b)>f⁡(c)f(b)>f(c). Hence

f[1]​(aε,b)=f⁡(b)−f⁡(aε)b−aε≥f⁡(b)−f⁡(c)b−a>0.f^{[1]}(a_{\varepsilon},b)=\frac{f(b)-f(a_{\varepsilon})}{b-a_{\varepsilon}}\geq\frac{f(b)-f(c)}{b-a}>0\,.

Therefore, for ε>0\varepsilon>0 sufficiently small,

f′​(aε)​f′​(b)−f[1]​(aε,b)2=ϵ​f′​(b)−f[1]​(aε,b)2<0.f^{\prime}(a_{\varepsilon})f^{\prime}(b)-f^{[1]}(a_{\varepsilon},b)^{2}=\epsilon f^{\prime}(b)-f^{[1]}(a_{\varepsilon},b)^{2}<0\,.

Thus Lf​(aε,b){\rm L}_{f}(a_{\varepsilon},b) is not positive semidefinite and

f′​(aε)​f′​(b)>0.f^{\prime}(a_{\varepsilon})f^{\prime}(b)>0\,.

The case f′​(a)>0f^{\prime}(a)>0 and f′​(b)=0f^{\prime}(b)=0 is analogous. Finally, suppose that

f′​(a)=f′​(b)=0.f^{\prime}(a)=f^{\prime}(b)=0\,.

Again, by the mean value theorem there exists c∈(a,b)c\in\left(a,b\right) such that

f′​(c)=f[1]​(a,b)>0.f^{\prime}(c)=f^{[1]}(a,b)>0\,.

Choose points c1,c2c_{1},c_{2} such that

a<c1<c<c2<ba<c_{1}<c<c_{2}<b

and

f′​(c1)>0,f′​(c2)>0.f^{\prime}(c_{1})>0\,,\qquad f^{\prime}(c_{2})>0\,.

By Darboux’s theorem, for every sufficiently small ε>0\varepsilon>0 there exist

aε∈(a,c1),bε∈(c2,b)a_{\varepsilon}\in\left(a,c_{1}\right)\,,\qquad b_{\varepsilon}\in\left(c_{2},b\right)

such that

f′​(aε)=f′​(bε)=ε.f^{\prime}(a_{\varepsilon})=f^{\prime}(b_{\varepsilon})=\varepsilon\,.

Since ff is increasing and c1<c2c_{1}<c_{2},

f[1]​(aε,bε)≥f⁡(c2)−f⁡(c1)b−a>0.f^{[1]}(a_{\varepsilon},b_{\varepsilon})\geq\frac{f(c_{2})-f(c_{1})}{b-a}>0\,.

Therefore, for ε>0\varepsilon>0 sufficiently small,

f′​(aε)​f′​(bε)−f[1]​(aε,bε)2=ε2−f[1]​(aε,bε)2<0.f^{\prime}(a_{\varepsilon})f^{\prime}(b_{\varepsilon})-f^{[1]}(a_{\varepsilon},b_{\varepsilon})^{2}=\varepsilon^{2}-f^{[1]}(a_{\varepsilon},b_{\varepsilon})^{2}<0\,.

Hence Lf​(aε,bε){\rm L}_{f}(a_{\varepsilon},b_{\varepsilon}) is not positive semidefinite and

f′​(aε)​f′​(bε)>0.f^{\prime}(a_{\varepsilon})f^{\prime}(b_{\varepsilon})>0\,.

Thus, whenever ff fails to be matrix monotone of degree 22, we can find a pair satisfying the hypotheses of the preceding proposition. It follows that ff is not radially convex of order 22 with respect to d∥⋅∥,f{\rm d}_{\|\cdot\|,f}. Therefore, radial convexity of order 22 implies matrix monotonicity of degree 22 .
